global.headline: TRUMP SUSPENDS THE SANCTIONS LAW HIS OWN PARTY PASSED 86–11, TWO DAYS BEFORE IT WOULD HAVE BITTEN
summary: An executive order signed late on Friday waived the Russia provisions of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 — which Trump signed into law in mid-September and the Senate passed 86–11 — two days before they took effect. Gone are tariffs of up to 100% on the largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, sanctions on Russia's energy sector, banks and shadow tanker fleet, and curbs on Russian sovereign debt and US investment; so is the clause making relief conditional on a peace deal Ukraine accepted. The order has no expiry; the White House said enforcement would impede peace efforts.

Zelensky said it "definitely helps only the Russians" and that "a US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin" only encourages more attacks, with further relief to follow; Russia struck more than 15 power generation and transmission sites on Friday. Thom Tillis called the order "beyond irresponsible", but Congress is in recess until after the 3 November election; Moscow's investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev called it "a truly historic moment". Zelensky added that Starshield terminals still cut out above 161kmh inside Ukraine yet ran beyond 180kmh when driven into the EU: "this is a planned operation".
global.geopolitical: The main economic lever against Moscow is off at one signature, nine days after Washington agreed to buy Russian diesel, and with the Ukrainian-consent condition deleted, nothing is left to trade for a settlement.
global.socioeconomic: The purpose is pump prices before 3 November: a 100% tariff on Chinese and Indian buyers of Russian crude would have pushed Brent past Friday's US$109.86 (S$140.62) settle, with US petrol already up 9.1% in September.

global.headline: FRANCE'S SCHOOL PROTESTS BECOME A COST-OF-LIVING REVOLT, AND SATURDAY ENDS WITH A TOWN HALL BURNT DOWN
summary: The interior ministry counted 550,000 people on the streets of France on Saturday, 110,000 in Paris; the CGT union said 800,000. The movement began last month in schools in Paris's poor northern suburbs over absent teachers and decrepit buildings and has widened, via social-media calls to revive the 2018 gilets jaunes, into a revolt over prices, fuel costs and fraying public services, with the CGT demanding "higher wages and pensions, lower prices".

Limoges' 143-year-old town hall burned and its roof collapsed, protesters rammed their way into Marseille's city hall, Lyon's tourist office was torched, and police fired teargas around Place de la République at masked groups who attacked a bank and looted shops. A demonstrator in Saint-Étienne lost a hand. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez first reported 400 arrests, mostly adults and "opportunistic delinquents who had seen a chance to pillage and loot", with more than 1,000 by late evening and at least 60 officers hurt; he ruled out a state of emergency. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu blamed the far left and said the government would not be "intimidated" by a "warm-up" for next year's presidential election. Belgium, Portugal and Italy had smaller cost-of-living protests the same day.
global.geopolitical: The EU's second economy is fighting its own streets months before a presidential election, which narrows what Paris can promise Kyiv as Washington drops its sanctions pressure — and the same grievance surfaced in three other EU states on one Saturday.
global.socioeconomic: A complaint about school maintenance is now a wages-and-prices movement with union backing: the fuel shock driving American inflation is now a political cost in Europe, and the burnt public buildings come out of the same strained budgets.

global.headline: THE UAE RETURNS TO THE YEMEN WAR UNDER SAUDI AIR COVER, AND EGYPT'S PARLIAMENT VOTES ON JOINING
summary: The UAE has agreed to resume payments to southern Yemeni government forces — mainly the Giant Brigades it funded until it quit the war in January — in return for Saudi air cover, according to sources in Yemen. It is the first tangible repair of the Saudi–Emirati rift over Yemen, forced by Houthi advances that have left Riyadh under daily drone and missile attack with airports and some energy infrastructure immobilised. Two Houthi missiles hit Aden airport on Friday, 500m from a Yemenia aircraft preparing to take off, a day after five people were killed at the presidential palace there.

At a military academy graduation on Saturday, President Abdel Fatah al-Sisi asked Egypt's parliament to sit in emergency session and authorise the defence of Saudi Arabia if asked: "I am speaking only for defence." Article 152 requires two-thirds of the House to send troops abroad, and the session is set for Sunday. Britain has sent an RAF Voyager tanker and is weighing a wider Saudi request. The Security Council affirmed Saudi self-defence on 15 October; the UN counts more than 200,000 people displaced since August and no reliable death toll.
global.geopolitical: A Gulf proxy fight is becoming an Arab coalition war, and Sunday's two-thirds vote in Cairo is the formal threshold for the first non-Gulf army to enter it. The reconciliation underneath it was bought by Houthi battlefield gains, not diplomacy.
global.socioeconomic: Re-funding the Giant Brigades restores the only effective anti-Houthi ground force, but the prizes contested are Taiz and Marib, and 200,000 people displaced since August are landing on aid agencies in an Aden whose airport and palace are both targets.

global.headline: ISRAELI SETTLERS BEAT A FRENCH MAYOR AND ATTACK THREE COUNTRIES' CONSULS DURING THE OLIVE HARVEST
summary: Seven masked men, some with clubs, attacked a diplomatic party in Taybeh in the occupied West Bank on Saturday, injuring three. Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was wearing his sash of office and getting into a car with diplomatic plates when he was knocked to the ground; his assailant shouted "Vive la France". His wife and Vincent Dollmann, archbishop of Cambrai, were threatened; an armoured Belgian mission car had its window smashed. The party had joined the olive harvest with France's consul general in Jerusalem and the Belgian and Polish consuls. The settlers had first attacked harvesters lower down the slope, assaulting a woman in her 70s and beating a man who needed six stitches.

Belgium's deputy prime minister and foreign minister Maxime Prévot said diplomatic work and olive harvesting "should never put anyone at risk of attack", and that Belgium will keep pressing for EU sanctions on settlers. Taybeh's priest, Father Bashar Fawadleh, said settlers had never before targeted foreign diplomats there. Yesh Din counts more than 170 settler attacks since 27 September, which Palestinian authorities say killed four people, injured more than 100 and damaged thousands of trees; Israel has also barred Palestinians from trees in Area C. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar condemned the attack and opened a police investigation, while warning diplomats they risk assault if they travel without military coordination.
global.geopolitical: Assaulting accredited consuls and a serving French mayor turns settler violence from a Palestinian grievance into a consular incident for France, Belgium and Poland, and hands Belgium's push for EU settler sanctions the precedent it lacked.
global.socioeconomic: The olive harvest is the West Bank's cash crop as much as its cultural season: 170 attacks in three weeks, thousands of damaged trees and the Area C exclusion take out a year's income for farming families.

global.headline: KENYA'S EBOLA OUTBREAK TURNS INWARD: FOUR NEW CASES, THREE OF THEM THE STAFF WHO TREATED PATIENT ONE
summary: Kenya's health ministry confirmed four new Bundibugyo Ebola cases on Saturday, taking the total to seven and marking the first transmission known to have occurred inside the country. Three are health workers — two men and a woman, aged 29, 35 and 32 — who managed the index patient on 3 and 4 October and had been quarantined since 9 October; the fourth is a male relative quarantined since 6 October. All four were already in quarantine when symptoms appeared. The ministry says 128 of 130 contacts, 98.5%, are traced and quarantined, above the 85% benchmark it considers necessary to break transmission, and that "the risk to the general public remains low".

The index patient was ill in Congo for about a month before travelling by road to Uganda and flying into Nairobi on 3 October; he died on 5 October, raising questions about screening at the Congo–Uganda border, closed since May, and at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport. There is no approved vaccine or treatment for the Bundibugyo strain. Kenya's cases trace to Congo's epidemic, the second largest recorded, with over 9,000 cases and 4,000 deaths.
global.geopolitical: A strain with no vaccine has reached East Africa's main air hub through a border formally closed since May, which makes Nairobi's screening — not Congo's containment — the question other governments will now put.
global.socioeconomic: Three of the four new patients are the clinicians who treated the first: the quickest way for an outbreak to strip a hospital of the staff who handle it, and Kenya has no licensed drug to protect them with.

singapore.headline: PM WONG FLIES TO QATAR AND THE UAE TODAY, HIS FIRST MIDDLE EAST TRIP AS PRIME MINISTER
summary: The Prime Minister's Office said on Saturday that Lawrence Wong will be in Doha from 18 to 20 October and in Abu Dhabi and Dubai from 20 to 22 October, invited by Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani and UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. In Qatar he will co-chair the ninth Qatar–Singapore High-Level Joint Committee with the Emir; the committee, set up in 2006 to steer the relationship, last met in Singapore in August 2023. The visits let Singapore exchange views on Middle East developments, reaffirm support for dialogue and diplomacy, and deepen cooperation in energy security and economic resilience, the PMO said.
singapore.geopolitical: Singapore is sending its head of government into the Gulf while its own advisory tells citizens to defer all travel to Saudi Arabia and a Singapore-flagged ship lies sunk off Hormuz — a test of what a small state's insistence on dialogue buys in a war it cannot influence.
singapore.socioeconomic: Energy security is the live item: Qatar is a principal LNG supplier to Asia, and the Q3 electricity tariff's record 31.91 cents/kWh before GST showed households here precisely what Gulf disruption costs them.

singapore.headline: THE WMO CALLS THIS ONE OF THE WORST HAZE EPISODES ON RECORD AND WARNS IT COULD RUN FOR MONTHS
summary: Ben Churchill, who directs the World Meteorological Organisation's regional office for Asia and the Pacific, said South-east Asia is in one of the worst transboundary haze episodes caused by Indonesian fires, hitting Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines alike, and that it could last weeks or even months until the winds shift and rain reaches the fires. The El Nino now under way is on track to be the strongest ever observed and has coincided with the dry season, creating what he called "the perfect storm" for fires lit by slash-and-burn clearing. He urged ASEAN to pool firefighting resources, improve warnings and change land practices.

Singapore has now had 13 consecutive days of unhealthy PSI readings, its longest run since 2015, with the 24-hour index still unhealthy on Saturday and hourly PM2.5 high. Grace Fu had warned on Friday that readings could reach hazardous and that relief depends on lighter, more variable winds three to four weeks away, with a fuller reprieve only when the winds turn northerly near the year's end.
singapore.geopolitical: An ASEAN resource-pooling proposal from the UN's weather agency reframes the episode: Singapore's legal notices to seven Indonesian companies address blame, but Malaysia and the Philippines breathe the same smoke and no regional firefighting capability exists to send.
singapore.socioeconomic: Months rather than weeks changes the arithmetic for employers, schools and anyone with a respiratory condition: 13 unhealthy days have already forced closures and exam contingencies, and the first improvement is three to four weeks out.

singapore.headline: SM LEE TELLS PORT WORKERS RIVAL PORTS ARE CATCHING UP FAST AND EMBODIED AI IS COMING FOR DECK JOBS
summary: At the Singapore Port Workers Union's 80th anniversary dinner on Saturday, Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong said rival ports are closing the gap fast on digitalisation and automation, while supply-chain disruption, climate change and geopolitical tension bear on every operator. Green fuels such as ammonia and methanol will demand new processes, skills and safety protocols, and AI, autonomous vehicles, sensors and robotics are already transforming operations — repetitive deck tasks such as coning and de-coning may in future be done by embodied artificial intelligence. He called for a renewed tripartite compact: "As in past waves of transformation, we must not leave workers to face these changes alone", to build "a disciplined and skilled workforce with a strong Singapore core". The union, founded in 1946, represents over 10,000 members at PSA Corporation, PSA International and port logistics firms; Singapore handled a record 44.66 million containers in 2025, up from 41.12 million.
singapore.geopolitical: Singapore's hold on transhipment rests on being the most reliable node rather than the cheapest, and the warning lands in a year when record throughput was manufactured by other people's disruption — Hormuz and the Red Sea rerouting cargo through it.
singapore.socioeconomic: Ten thousand workers are being told their jobs change again, from crane cabs to supervising machines; the tripartite compact is how Singapore has historically repriced that transition without industrial action.

singapore.headline: SINGAPORE ACCREDITS ITS FIRST FIVE TCM PROVIDERS AND WILL STUDY LETTING THEM ORDER X-RAYS
summary: Health Minister Ong Ye Kung launched a voluntary accreditation framework for traditional Chinese medicine at the 23rd World Congress of Chinese Medicine on Saturday, naming the first five accredited providers: Kwong Wai Shiu TCM Centre, NTU Chinese Medicine, the headquarters of Singapore Chung Hwa and Thong Chai Medical Institutions, and Thomson Chinese Medicine. Run by the Academy of Chinese Medicine, Singapore, it lasts three years for clinics and two for practitioners and sits above the existing duty to register with the TCM Practitioners Board. "Our objective is to establish accreditation as something beyond licence of practice", Ong said. The ministry will study whether accredited practitioners working with GPs may order X-rays, and opens a second call for its TCM Integrative Sandbox on 3 November; the first chose seven acupuncture projects from 18 proposals, and treatments proving clinically and cost-effective over one to two years can be funded more widely.
singapore.geopolitical: Hosting the world congress and publishing a standard on the same day positions Singapore as the place that writes the rules for integrative medicine in Asia — a quieter form of influence than it looks.
singapore.socioeconomic: An X-ray ordering right and a sandbox that ends in public funding would move TCM from out-of-pocket spending towards subsidised care: the first real cost shift for treatments many Singaporeans already pay for privately.

word.definition: An edict issued by an arbitrary authority; originally a decree of the Russian tsar or government carrying the force of law.
word.etymology: From Russian ukaz, 'decree', from ukazat', 'to show, to order'. It entered English in the early 18th century through travellers' accounts of Peter the Great, whose published edicts were the first ukases English readers met.
word.example: Congress passed the Graham Act 86–11 and the president signed it; a single Friday-night ukase suspended it two days before it would have bitten, and Moscow's investment envoy called the moment historic.
